tagline: The story of a prophet who ran from God's call, was swallowed and spared, preached to Israel's enemies, and was angry when God showed them mercy.
overview:
Jonah is unlike the other prophetic books. Most of them are collections of oracles with a little narrative; Jonah is almost entirely narrative, with only one short sentence of prophecy (3:4). It tells of Jonah son of Amittai, a prophet of Israel, whom God sends to preach against Nineveh, a great city of Assyria. Jonah runs the other way, boarding a ship for Tarshish at the far end of the known world. God hurls a storm at the sea, the pagan sailors throw Jonah overboard at his own request, and a great fish swallows him. From inside the fish he prays a psalm of thanksgiving, and the fish puts him out on dry land.

Given a second chance, Jonah goes to Nineveh and announces that in forty days it will be overturned. To everyone's surprise but God's, the whole city repents, from the king to the cattle, and God relents from the disaster he threatened. The last chapter is the real climax. Jonah is furious, and he explains why he ran in the first place: he knew God was gracious and compassionate and would forgive. God gives him a plant for shade, then takes it away, and ends the book with a question that Jonah never answers: should God not care about a great city full of people and animals?

Jonah matters because it turns the prophetic message back on the prophet and on the reader. The pagans in this book (sailors, a king, a whole city) respond to God more readily than God's own prophet does. The book asks whether we want God's mercy for ourselves only, and whether we can bear to see it given to people we fear or hate.
author: The book does not name its author. It tells the story about Jonah in the third person rather than in his own voice. Older Jewish and Christian tradition often assumed Jonah wrote it himself or that it came from prophetic circles close to him. Most modern scholars think it was written by an unnamed author some time after the events it describes, pointing to features of its Hebrew (some words and constructions more common in later Hebrew and Aramaic), to the description of Nineveh in the past tense ("Now Nineveh was an exceedingly great city", 3:3), and to its reflective, carefully crafted form. Others answer that the linguistic evidence is inconclusive, since northern Israelite Hebrew may account for some unusual forms, and that the past tense can simply be narrative style.
date: The events are set in the eighth century BC. Jonah son of Amittai is mentioned in 2 Kings 14:25 as a prophet from Gath-hepher in Galilee who foretold the expansion of Israel's borders under King Jeroboam II (about 793 to 753 BC). The date of writing is debated. Those who read the book as written by Jonah or near his time place it in the eighth century. Many scholars date it after the exile, often in the fifth or fourth century BC, citing its language and its concern with how Israel should regard the nations, a live question in the Persian period. Others place it in between, in the seventh or sixth century. Whatever the date of writing, the story is set while Nineveh was still standing and powerful, as it was until the Babylonians and Medes destroyed it in 612 BC.
setting:
In the eighth century BC Assyria, centered on the upper Tigris River in what is now northern Iraq, was the rising power of the ancient Near East. Its kings campaigned west toward Syria and the Mediterranean coast and were known for brutal treatment of conquered peoples. Nineveh was one of its great cities; it became the royal capital under Sennacherib around 700 BC. For Israel, Assyria was the enemy that would destroy the northern kingdom and its capital Samaria in 722 BC and later invade Judah. The prophet Nahum would celebrate Nineveh's fall.

The book's other places mark the edges of Jonah's world. Joppa (modern Jaffa, near Tel Aviv) was a port on Israel's coast. Tarshish lay far to the west; it is often identified with Tartessus in southern Spain, though some suggest Sardinia or another western site. To flee to Tarshish was to go as far from Nineveh, which lay to the east, as a ship could take you.
purpose: The book is aimed at readers who, like Jonah, know the right creed about God but resent its implications. Jonah can quote Israel's confession that God is "gracious and compassionate" (4:2, echoing Exodus 34:6), yet he is angry that this grace reaches Nineveh. The book shows God's concern for all people, including Israel's enemies, and it shows that God's warnings of judgment are meant to lead to repentance. Whether written in the eighth century for a prosperous Israel under Jeroboam II or in the Persian period for a community debating its relationship with the nations, it calls God's people to share God's own compassion. The open question at the end is addressed as much to the reader as to Jonah.
story: Jonah lived in the period covered by 2 Kings 14, when the northern kingdom of Israel enjoyed a last season of prosperity under Jeroboam II, the same years in which Amos and Hosea preached. Within a few decades Assyria would destroy that kingdom. In the canon Jonah stands fifth among the twelve Minor Prophets, between Obadiah (a judgment on Edom) and Micah. Its theme reaches back to God's promise that all the families of the earth would be blessed through Abraham (Genesis 12:3) and forward to the church's mission to the nations. Jonah's reluctance also anticipates the tension in Acts over whether Gentiles could be welcomed as they were.
christ:
Jesus himself used this book. When his opponents demanded a sign, he answered that "none will be given it except the sign of the prophet Jonah" (Matthew 12:39). He explained: "For as Jonah was three days and three nights in the belly of the great fish, so the Son of Man will be three days and three nights in the heart of the earth" (Matthew 12:40). Jonah's descent and deliverance became a picture of Jesus' death, burial, and resurrection. Jesus also pointed to the Ninevites' repentance as a judgment on his own hearers, adding "now One greater than Jonah is here" (Matthew 12:41; compare Luke 11:29-32).

The contrasts are as important as the likeness. Jonah was thrown into the sea for his own disobedience, and his willingness to die saved the sailors almost despite himself; Jesus went into death in obedience and for others. Jonah resented God's mercy to the nations; Jesus wept over a city and sent his followers to all nations. The book's closing question about God's compassion is answered in the gospel, where God does not merely spare a city but gives his Son for the world.
reading:
Jonah is a carefully told story, full of irony, repetition, and surprise. Notice the word "great", which describes the city, the wind, the storm, the sailors' fear, the fish, Jonah's anger, and his joy. Notice how often Jonah goes "down" as he flees, and how God "appoints" a fish, a plant, a worm, and a wind. Notice that the pagans (sailors, king, city) are consistently more responsive to God than the prophet is. The book ends with a question, and the reader is meant to feel its weight.

The great debate about Jonah concerns its genre. Many readers, Jewish and Christian, have taken it as historical narrative: Jonah is a real prophet known from 2 Kings 14:25, the story is told as events, and Jesus refers to Jonah and to the Ninevites as he refers to other historical figures, placing the men of Nineveh at the final judgment alongside the queen of the South. Many other scholars, including some who hold a high view of Scripture, read it as a didactic story or parable, pointing to its symmetry, its humor and exaggeration (fasting cattle in sackcloth), the lack of a named Assyrian king, and the absence of any Assyrian record of a mass repentance. They argue that Jesus could use a well-known story as an illustration without settling its genre. A third group holds both: a historical prophet and real events told with deliberate literary artistry and a teaching purpose. Whatever position a reader takes, the book's message is the same, and the worst misreading is to argue about the fish and miss the question about mercy with which the book ends.

structure.title: Jonah runs, and the sailors fear the LORD
structure.summary: Jonah flees toward Tarshish. God sends a storm, the sailors throw Jonah into the sea, the sea grows calm, and the sailors worship the LORD. A great fish swallows Jonah.

structure.title: Jonah's prayer from the depths
structure.summary: From inside the fish Jonah prays a psalm of thanksgiving for rescue from death. The fish puts him out on dry land.

structure.title: Nineveh repents
structure.summary: Jonah preaches a five-word warning in Hebrew. The whole city, led by its king, fasts and turns from violence, and God relents.

structure.title: Jonah's anger and God's question
structure.summary: Jonah is furious at God's mercy. God uses a plant, a worm, and a hot wind to teach him, and ends with a question about his compassion for Nineveh.

themes.title: God's compassion for the nations
themes.body: The book's final verse is its thesis: God cares about the great city of Nineveh, its people who cannot tell their right hand from their left, and even its cattle. God's mercy is not the property of Israel. The sailors and the Ninevites, outsiders all, turn to him and are received.

themes.title: The reluctant prophet
themes.body: Jonah is not a hero. He runs, sleeps through the storm, preaches the shortest sermon in the prophets, and then sulks when it works. The book holds him up as a mirror to God's people, who can confess God's grace in words and resent it in practice.

themes.title: Judgment and repentance
themes.body: Jonah's message, "Forty more days and Nineveh will be overturned", contains no offer of mercy, yet the Ninevites repent in hope, and God relents. The book shows that God's announcements of judgment are often conditional, meant to bring people to turn (as Jeremiah 18:7-8 explains). The Hebrew word for overturned can also mean turned around, and Nineveh is overturned, though not in the way Jonah expected.

themes.title: God's sovereignty over creation
themes.body: The LORD whom Jonah confesses as the God "who made the sea and the dry land" (1:9) commands wind, sea, fish, plant, worm, and east wind. Everything in the book obeys God except his prophet.

themes.title: Death and deliverance
themes.body: Jonah goes down to the depths, to the edge of Sheol, and God brings him up. His psalm in chapter 2 gives thanks for rescue from death, a pattern Jesus took up as a sign of his own death and resurrection.

keyChapters.why: Jonah's flight and the pagan sailors' turn to the LORD set up the book's central irony.
Jonah's prayer from the fish, the basis of Jesus' sign of Jonah, confesses that salvation is from the LORD.
Nineveh's repentance and God's relenting show that judgment announced is meant to lead to turning.
Jonah's anger at God's grace and God's closing question are the heart of the book.

parts.body:
Jonah is the fifth of the twelve shorter prophets, and it is unlike the others. Most of them are collections of oracles with a little story. Jonah is almost all story, four chapters with only one short sentence of prophecy (3:4).

God sends Jonah son of Amittai, a prophet of Israel, to preach against Nineveh, a great city of Assyria. Jonah runs the other way, boarding a ship for Tarshish at the far end of the known world. God hurls a storm at the sea, the sailors throw Jonah overboard at his own request, and a great fish swallows him. From inside the fish he prays, and the fish puts him out on dry land.

Sent a second time, Jonah goes to Nineveh and announces, “Forty more days and Nineveh will be overturned!” (3:4). The whole city repents, from the king to the cattle, and God relents. The last chapter is the real climax. Jonah is furious, and he finally says why he ran: he knew God was gracious and compassionate and would forgive. The book ends with God's question, which Jonah never answers: ‘So should I not care about the great city of Nineveh’ (4:11)?

parts.h: Where it sits in the story
parts.body:
Jonah lived in the years covered by 2 Kings 14, when the northern kingdom had a last season of prosperity under Jeroboam II, the same years in which Amos and Hosea preached. Second Kings names him: Jeroboam restored Israel's border ‘according to the word that the LORD, the God of Israel, had spoken through His servant Jonah son of Amittai, the prophet from Gath-hepher’ (2 Kings 14:25). Within a few decades Assyria, Nineveh's empire, would destroy that kingdom.

In the order of the Twelve, Jonah stands between Obadiah, a judgment on Edom, and Micah. Its theme reaches back to God's promise that all the families of the earth would find good through Abraham, and forward to the church's mission to the nations, and to the struggle in Acts over whether Gentiles could be welcomed as they were.

The book does not name its author, and it tells the story about Jonah in the third person. Older Jewish and Christian tradition often assumed that Jonah wrote it, or that it came from prophets close to him. Most modern scholars think an unnamed author wrote it some time later. They point to features of its Hebrew more common in later Hebrew and Aramaic, to Nineveh described in the past tense (3:3), and to its carefully crafted form. Others answer that the language evidence is inconclusive, since northern Hebrew may explain some unusual forms, and that the past tense can simply be the way stories are told.

The events are set in the eighth century BC. The site's guide to the kings places Jonah's ministry within Jeroboam II's reign, 793 to 753 BC. The date of writing is debated. Those who think Jonah or someone near him wrote it place it in the eighth century. Many scholars date it after the exile, often in the fifth or fourth century BC, pointing to its language and its concern with how Israel should regard the nations. Others place it in the seventh or sixth century. Whatever the date of writing, the story is set while Nineveh still stood, as it did until it was destroyed in 612 BC.

The great debate about Jonah is what kind of writing it is, and this site takes no side.

Many readers, Jewish and Christian, have taken it as history. Jonah is a real prophet known from 2 Kings 14:25, the story is told as events, and Jesus speaks of Jonah and the Ninevites as he speaks of other figures of history, placing the men of Nineveh at the final judgment beside the queen of the South.

Many other scholars, some who hold a high view of Scripture among them, read it as a teaching story or parable. They point to its balanced shape, its humor and exaggeration, such as cattle fasting in sackcloth, the absence of any named Assyrian king, and the absence of any Assyrian record of a mass repentance. They argue that Jesus could use a well-known story as an illustration without settling its genre.

A third group holds both: a historical prophet and real events, told with deliberate artistry and a teaching purpose.

Whatever position a reader takes, the book's message is the same. The worst misreading is to argue about the fish and miss the question about mercy with which the book ends.

In the eighth century BC Assyria, centered on the upper Tigris River in what is now northern Iraq, was the rising power of the ancient Near East. Its kings campaigned west toward Syria and the coast and were known for brutal treatment of conquered peoples. Nineveh was one of its great cities, and it became the royal capital under Sennacherib around 700 BC. For Israel, Assyria was the enemy that would destroy Samaria in 722 BC and later invade Judah. Nahum would announce Nineveh's fall.

Joppa, modern Jaffa near Tel Aviv, was a port on Israel's coast. Tarshish lay far to the west. It is often identified with Tartessus in southern Spain, though some suggest Sardinia or another western site. Nineveh lay to the east. To flee to Tarshish was to go as far from Nineveh as a ship could take you.

The book has two halves that mirror each other. In chapters 1 and 2, the word of the LORD comes to Jonah, he runs, pagan sailors turn to God, and Jonah prays. In chapters 3 and 4, the word comes a second time, he goes, pagan Ninevites turn to God, and Jonah prays again, this time in anger.

It is told with irony, repetition and surprise. Notice the word great, which describes the city, the wind, the storm, the sailors' fear, the fish, Jonah's anger and his joy. Notice how often Jonah goes down as he flees: down to Joppa, down into the ship, down into the sea. Notice that God appoints a fish, a plant, a worm and a wind. And notice that the pagans, sailors, a king, a city, keep responding to God more readily than his prophet.

‘Jonah, however, got up to flee to Tarshish, away from the presence of the LORD’ (1:3). He does not say why until chapter 4. The LORD hurls a great wind on the sea, and the sailors cry each to his own god while Jonah sleeps below deck. They cast lots, the lot falls on Jonah, and he confesses: ‘I worship the LORD, the God of the heavens, who made the sea and the dry land’ (1:9).

He tells them to throw him into the sea. The sailors try to row back to land, then pray to the LORD not to hold them guilty, and throw him over. The sea grows calm. ‘Then the men feared the LORD greatly’ (1:16), and offered sacrifices and vows. The LORD appoints a great fish to swallow Jonah, and he is in its belly three days and three nights (1:17).

From inside the fish Jonah prays a psalm of thanks. He describes sinking into the deep, cast out of God's sight, seaweed wrapped around his head, and God bringing his life up from the pit. It ends, ‘Salvation is from the LORD’ (2:9). Then the fish puts him out on dry land.

parts.h: Forty days, and a city that turned
parts.body:
The word of the LORD comes to Jonah a second time, and this time he goes. Nineveh is an exceedingly great city, three days' walk across. Jonah goes one day's walk in and gives his message. ‘And the Ninevites believed God’ (3:5). They call a fast and put on sackcloth, from the greatest to the least.

The king rises from his throne, puts on sackcloth and sits in ashes. He decrees that people and animals alike must fast, call on God and turn from violence: ‘Who knows? God may turn and relent’ (3:9). When God sees that they have turned from their evil ways, ‘He relented from the disaster He had threatened to bring upon them’ (3:10).

Was Jonah's prophecy false, since Nineveh was not destroyed in forty days? The book's own answer is in God's character: his warnings carry an unspoken condition, as Jeremiah says, and turning changes the outcome. Some also note that the word overturned can mean turned around, so that the city was indeed overturned, in repentance.

Jonah is not glad. He is furious. ‘I knew that You are a gracious and compassionate God, slow to anger, abounding in loving devotion’ (4:2), he prays, the words God spoke of himself at Sinai, now thrown back at him as a complaint. Then he asks to die, and God asks, ‘Have you any right to be angry?’ (4:4).

Jonah sits east of the city to see what will happen. God appoints a plant to shade him, and Jonah is very glad. Then God appoints a worm to kill the plant, and a scorching east wind, and Jonah again wishes to die. God says that Jonah cared about a plant he did not tend or grow. ‘So should I not care about the great city of Nineveh, which has more than 120,000 people who cannot tell their right hand from their left, and many cattle as well?’ (4:11).

The book ends there, with God's question and no answer from Jonah. The reader is left to answer it. Jonah's wish to die is recorded honestly, and God meets it with questions and patience, not contempt.

If you have thoughts of hurting yourself, speak to someone today: a doctor, a pastor, a trusted friend, or a crisis line in your country. If you are in danger right now, call your local emergency number. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.

parts.h: How the New Testament reads Jonah
parts.body:
Jesus himself used this book. When his opponents demanded a sign, he said that ‘none will be given it except the sign of the prophet Jonah’ (Matthew 12:39). ‘For as Jonah was three days and three nights in the belly of the great fish, so the Son of Man will be three days and three nights in the heart of the earth’ (Matthew 12:40). Jonah's going down and coming up became a picture of Jesus' death, burial and rising.

Jesus also pointed to the Ninevites' repentance as a judgment on his own hearers: ‘they repented at the preaching of Jonah, and now One greater than Jonah is here’ (Matthew 12:41). Luke records the same words: ‘For as Jonah was a sign to the Ninevites, so the Son of Man will be a sign to this generation’ (Luke 11:30).

These are the New Testament's lines from Jonah, and these notes draw no others. Jonah's resentment of mercy to his enemies is a warning to every reader, and the New Testament never uses it to blame the Jewish people.

Read Jonah as a story, and enjoy it. It is funny in places and painful in others. Watch the prophet more than the fish.

Read it as a mirror. The book turns the prophet's message back on the prophet and on the reader. It asks whether you want God's mercy for yourself only, and whether you can bear to see it given to people you fear or hate.

And read it to the end. The book stops on a question, and the question is addressed to whoever is reading.

teaching.mapNote: Two places are drawn. Joppa is at the point this site's map of Acts uses. Nineveh is drawn at its ruin mounds, Kuyunjik and Nebi Yunus, on the east bank of the Tigris opposite Mosul. Tarshish is left off, because where it lay is disputed: Tartessus in Spain, Sardinia and other western sites have been proposed. No borders are drawn. The map makes no claim about any border today.
